title: Judges 13:1–7
context: Judges 13 begins the Samson cycle. Israel again does evil and is under Philistine rule for forty years. The angel of the LORD appears to the barren wife of Manoah, a Danite from Zorah, and announces a son who will be a Nazirite from the womb and will begin to save Israel. The Nazirite rules echo Numbers 6. Some readers take the angel of the LORD as a theophany or a preincarnate appearance of Christ, while others see a created angel; the text does not settle this. Both traditions share the passage’s focus on God’s gracious initiative.

verses.text: The children of Israel again did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight; and the LORD delivered them into the hand of the Philistines forty years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel again does evil, and the LORD gives them into Philistine hands for forty years. Unlike some earlier cycles, the text does not mention Israel crying out to God (compare 3:9, 15).

Arminian readers see God responding to real choices with real consequences.
verses.reformedNotes:
The familiar pattern of sin and oppression returns. The Philistines now become Israel’s main threat.

Reformed readers see God acting to deliver even when his people do not ask. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s judgment and mercy in Judges.

verses.text: There was a certain man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah; and his wife was barren, and childless.
verses.arminianNotes:
Manoah of Zorah, a Danite, has a wife who is barren and childless. The story begins with a quiet household need.

Arminian readers see God noticing an ordinary family. The unnamed wife becomes central to the story.
verses.reformedNotes:
Barrenness recalls Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, and later Hannah. God often begins deliverance with an impossible birth.

Reformed readers see God’s initiative in bringing life where there was none. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s grace working through unlikely beginnings.

verses.text: The LORD’s angel appeared to the woman, and said to her, “See now, you are barren and childless; but you shall conceive and bear a son.
verses.arminianNotes:
The angel of the LORD appears to the woman and announces that she will conceive and bear a son. The message comes to her directly.

Arminian readers see God honoring the woman by speaking to her first.
verses.reformedNotes:
The announcement follows a pattern seen elsewhere in Scripture. God promises a son to a childless woman.

Reformed readers see God’s gracious initiative. Some in both traditions read the angel of the LORD as a theophany, others as a created angel; the text does not settle the question, and it is not settled here either.

verses.text: Now therefore please beware and drink no wine nor strong drink, and don’t eat any unclean thing;
verses.arminianNotes:
She must drink no wine or strong drink and eat nothing unclean. The mother shares in the child’s consecration.

Arminian readers see the calling beginning even before birth, with the parents invited into faithful obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
The restrictions echo the Nazirite rules of Numbers 6. The mother keeps them during pregnancy.

Reformed readers see God setting the child apart from the womb. Both traditions describe this constructively as a sign of consecration, a life marked out for God’s purpose.

verses.text: for, behold, you shall conceive and give birth to a son. No razor shall come on his head, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb. He shall begin to save Israel out of the hand of the Philistines.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The child will be a Nazirite from the womb, no razor on his head, and will begin to save Israel from the Philistines. His calling is lifelong.

Arminian readers note the word ‘begin’: Samson’s deliverance is partial, and the work continues after him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Unlike the voluntary, often temporary vow in Numbers 6, this Nazirite status is given by God from birth.

Reformed readers see God appointing a deliverer before he is born. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the full deliverance from the Philistines comes later in Israel’s history.

verses.text: Then the woman came and told her husband, saying, “A man of God came to me, and his face was like the face of the angel of God, very awesome. I didn’t ask him where he was from, neither did he tell me his name;
verses.arminianNotes:
The woman tells her husband that a man of God came, with a face like an angel of God, very awesome. She did not ask his name.

Arminian readers see her honest uncertainty about the visitor. She reports what she saw and heard.
verses.reformedNotes:
She describes him as both a man of God and awe-inspiring. His identity is not yet clear to her.

Reformed readers see the story building suspense about the visitor. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, without pressing a conclusion about the messenger’s identity.

verses.text: but he said to me, ‘Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son; and now drink no wine nor strong drink. Don’t eat any unclean thing, for the child shall be a Nazirite to God from the womb to the day of his death.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
She repeats the message, adding that the child will be a Nazirite ‘to the day of his death.’ The phrase anticipates the end of Samson’s story.

Arminian readers see the calling as lifelong, though Samson’s faithfulness to it will be uneven.
verses.reformedNotes:
Her retelling adds a note about his death that the angel’s words in verse 5 did not include. The narrator may be foreshadowing chapter 16.

Reformed readers likewise see the hint of what lies ahead. Both traditions share this reading.
